extracted.intended_audience: PR practitioners, business leaders, and organizations seeking practical lessons in crisis management
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and lessons drawn from real-world crisis management case studies for organizations and PR teams, describing core principles, elements, and leadership behaviors that constitute effective crisis response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication (timely and effective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely and effective communication is essential during a crisis; it involves keeping stakeholders informed and addressing their concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate quickly, honestly, and clearly to build or restore trust. Examples: Tylenol’s transparent public safety communications after tampering; United Airlines’ poor initial statement that worsened backlash. Includes social media responses — avoid statements that inflame public sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination (cross-stakeholder collaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper coordination ensures that all relevant parties work together efficiently to manage the crisis, making use of available resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate internal teams, suppliers, partners, and external agencies to ensure consistent actions and messaging. Example: KFC worked closely with suppliers and delivery partners to resolve supply-chain issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (clear plans and decision-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining control means having a clear plan, making informed decisions, and implementing strategies to mitigate the crisis's impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish command structures, decision rights, and contingency plans in advance so responses are decisive and organized rather than reactive or chaotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Containment (limit scope and escalation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Containment is about limiting the crisis’s scope and preventing it from escalating further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act immediately to isolate and limit harm (e.g., recalls, halting operations, blocking compromised systems). The page lists containment both as a core 'C' and as an element of crisis management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation (planning and rehearsals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting ready: create strategies, figure out actions, and practice with your team to be prepared for possible problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop crisis plans, playbooks, and run simulations so teams know roles and procedures before a crisis occurs. The page emphasizes preparation as the first of the five elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification (early warning and detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spotting the trouble: recognizing early warning signs of a problem before it gets worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor signals (social, operational, security, financial) to detect issues early. Early recognition enables faster containment and reduces overall impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution (repair and remediation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixing the problem: after containing the issue, implement a plan to correct and remediate damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate remediation steps, involve necessary experts, compensate affected parties where appropriate, and restore normal operations while documenting decisions and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning (post-crisis review and improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning: after the crisis, analyze what went wrong and what was done well to be better prepared next time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct postmortems, capture lessons learned, update plans and training, and implement systemic changes. The page lists Learning as the final element of crisis management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of case studies (breadth of incident types to consider)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case studies should cover a wide range of companies and crisis types, from large corporations to small nonprofits and incidents ranging from product recalls to cyberattacks and environmental accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include diverse examples—natural disasters, product safety issues/recalls, cyber attacks, reputation issues, pandemics, financial crises, PR messes, environmental accidents, workplace incidents, and legal/political troubles—to identify transferable patterns and tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case studies to identify patterns and adapt strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: By examining many cases you can find common patterns, learn from successes and failures, adapt strategies, and prepare in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract repeatable tactics and anti-patterns from multiple case studies to build a tailored crisis playbook. The page frames case studies as a 'playbook' for anticipating traps and choosing appropriate responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent, accountable responses protect trust; evasive or blame-shifting responses worsen crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit mistakes when appropriate, be open about actions taken, and accept responsibility where due. Contrast: Tylenol (transparent recall) vs. Volkswagen/Equifax (evasiveness or delayed, confusing communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed of response (act quickly but thoughtfully)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good leaders act quickly in emergencies—consider choices but avoid excessive delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiate immediate containment and communication actions; speed reduces escalation. Balance quick action with fact-gathering to avoid incorrect statements that could exacerbate the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy and tone in communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate clearly and kindly; care for those affected to create unity and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empathetic language, address affected parties’ concerns, and choose tone appropriate to the situation (e.g., KFC used honest, friendly tone and measured humor). Avoid flippant or defensive messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of tone and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone may be used strategically (e.g., KFC used humor successfully) but must be appropriate for the crisis context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience sentiment before using humor; where safety or severe harm is involved, prioritize seriousness and empathy over levity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media crisis management
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media requires swift, well-crafted responses because public sentiment can spread rapidly online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor platforms, respond promptly, correct misinformation, and avoid statements that inflame the situation. Example: United Airlines’ initial social-media statement worsened the crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership traits in crises (flexibility, persistence, decisive action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective crisis leaders are flexible, persistent, decisive, and able to inspire trust through communication and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders should adapt plans as situations evolve, remain steadfast under criticism, and direct teams with clarity. The page cites Churchill, Mandela, Jacinda Ardern, Elon Musk, and Dr. Fauci as illustrative leaders with relevant traits.
